5: 1. "Inputs" sheet: choose your business type. The prime cost target changes on its own (65% for full service, 55% for counter or self-service), and both targets are green cells you can adjust.
6: 2. Check the employer payroll taxes and benefits rate and your target food cost: the whole workbook reads those two cells.
7: 3. "Monthly" sheet: for each month, net food and beverage sales, beginning inventory, purchases, ending inventory, gross wages and other labor costs. All PRE-TAX.
8: 4. Product usage is calculated on its own: beginning inventory + purchases − ending inventory. It isn't the same as the month's purchases.
9: 5. Labor cost adds employer payroll taxes and benefits to gross wages: $15,400 of wages costs $20,482 with a 33% load. Counting gross wages alone is the most expensive mistake on this sheet.
10: 6. Read the "Prime cost" column: if it's above target, it turns red. The chart shows the twelve months against the target line.
11: 7. The TOTAL / AVERAGE row is a WEIGHTED average: it divides the year's usage by the year's sales; it doesn't average the twelve percentages.
13: All figures are PRE-TAX; amounts carry no currency symbol and are in your currency. Food cost and prime cost are measured on NET sales (before sales tax, VAT or GST, and without tips) and on cost NET of any tax you get back: in the US, sales tax you pay on supplies is a cost; if you're registered for VAT or GST/HST, the tax on purchases is cash flow, not cost.
14: Prime cost = product cost + labor cost with payroll taxes and benefits, over net sales. It's the metric that measures the health of the business because it brings together the two lines you can really move.
15: A "good" food cost can be hiding a broken labor cost: that's why the two columns sit together and the traffic light looks at the sum.
16: Margin after prime cost isn't profit: it hasn't paid rent, utilities, depreciation or taxes yet.
17: The "Product cost on total sales" column on this sheet is NOT the same number as the menu food cost % (menu-engineering-matrix.xlsx): here the usage of ALL product (food + beverage) is compared with TOTAL sales, because that's what prime cost needs. The matrix calculates the food cost of food ONLY, over food sales ONLY. Both are right; they measure different things.
